Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-08-19 15:00 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Neill (Redwood SE), Ravi Patel (Peregrine CTO), Sofia Alvarez (Peregrine Head of Platform), Ben Kim (Peregrine Sr SRE)

Summary: Quick kickoff to map out reliability requirements — multi-region routing desires, fallback policies, and SLA/escallation expectations. Goal: align on a pilot scope (hosted -> dedicated failover) and what benchmarks Peregrine wants.

Topics: routing policy, fallthrough tiers, regional failover, SLOs, encryption/KMS, SOC 2, canary rollouts, KV cache/in-memory behavior on failover.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining — I think we saw the calendar, uh, Ravi, Sofia, Ben — thanks for making time.
[00:06] Ravi Patel: Yeah thanks Maya, appreciate it. We're pretty tight on time window so we'll try to be concise. We're exploring Redwood because of your cost vs latency claims and because we need predictable failover for our customer-facing assistant.
[00:20] Maya Chen: Great. Liam from my team will walk through technical constraints and I'll handle the business/SLA parts. Liam over to you.
[00:27] Liam O'Neill: Cool. Quick caveat — transcript might garble a few product names. We'll say Redwood Hosted, Dedicated, Private. We often talk about prefix caching and KV cache; that's the key for keeping cold-starts low.
[00:39] Sofia Alvarez: Quick context — our assistant serves financial compliance queries; most traffic is US-east with 15% EU, spikey during market open. We need <150ms p50 for quick hits, p95 under 700ms ideally. We cannot have more than 2% error/failure to model.
[01:00] Ben Kim: Also on retention — logs must be segregated, and any customer data leaving our VPC needs to be audit-logged. SOC2 is table stakes, iso is preferable.
[01:12] Liam O'Neill: Understood. For multi-region: common pattern is active-passive with active in us-east and passive in eu-west, warmed by periodic heartbeats; or active-active with geo-DNS + smart routing. Tradeoffs are latency vs cost and complexity.
[01:30] Maya Chen: For Redwood Hosted we can do region routing and automatic fallback, but dedicated gives you pinned GPU pools and deterministic throughput. Private means you manage networking and we ship a control plane — different compliance envelope.
[01:45] Ravi Patel: We're leaning dedicated for predictable throughput but want hosted as fallback to avoid full customer impact if dedicated pool hits a Z-level problem. Is that supported?
[01:55] Liam O'Neill: Yes, we support cross-tier fallbacks. Typical policy is: primary -> Dedicated in us-east (pinned model); secondary -> Hosted regional variant with model quantized for cost; tertiary -> degraded text-only model for non-critical responses. You can configure thresholds (error rate, latency, queue length) to trigger fallthrough.
[02:20] Sofia Alvarez: How fast is the failover? We worry about KV cache loss causing long tails.
[02:26] Liam O'Neill: There's two parts: routing failover latency (DNS/edge re-route) and runtime state. For KV cache we do cold-warm strategies: prefix cache replication for recent contexts, and aggressive pre-warming during detected partial outage. In practice we see app-visible failover in 2-10s range depending on TTLs and routing choices.
[02:46] Ben Kim: 2-10s is a wide band — if market trading queries are affected for 10s that's bad. Can we do health probes plus sticky sessions to keep sessions pinned in failover?
[02:58] Liam O'Neill: Yes, you can reduce switchover by using active-passive with a low failover TTL and keepalive probes. Also we offer session affinity tokens so the KV cache can be rehydrated or served from a warmed standby.
[03:14] Maya Chen: On the SLA front — Hosted has publicised uptime targets, and Dedicated can get higher SLA with reserved capacity and on-call commitments. We can map incident severity to RTO/RPOs in the contract for an enterprise seat.
[03:30] Ravi Patel: What's typical RTO you offer for dedicated? We're thinking 30 minutes for sev1 failover to fallback tiers, and 4 hours for full recovery.
[03:38] Maya Chen: For Dedicated we usually promise a 15-30 minute automated reroute to fallback model, and 4 hours for full degraded recovery depending on the cause; we can negotiate tighter RTOs with support SLAs and runbook commitments.
[03:51] Sofia Alvarez: And how about data plane encryption and key management? We use AWS KMS + HSM for some customers.
[03:58] Liam O'Neill: Private and Dedicated support KMS/HSM integrations. Hosted can integrate via customer-managed keys for a private deployment; we also provide audit logs for all key ops. We'll share a SOC2/ISO excerpt after the call.
[04:12] Ravi Patel: Competitors sometimes require custom routing glue; can Redwood do automatic fallback without us adding extra routing layers?
[04:20] Liam O'Neill: Yes, our smart router can make per-request decisions — policies can be latency-first, cost-first, or region-first. It uses request metadata and runtime signals to choose target pool. There's also deterministic fallback ordering you tweak.
[04:33] Ben Kim: If the primary dedicated GPU pool runs out of capacity during a burst, is the fallback synchronous? I'm worried about token-level differences if the model variant is quantized.
[04:45] Liam O'Neill: The fallback is immediate in terms of request routing but you'll see model variant differences; we recommend non-critical responses use degraded variants. For critical workflows you can pin model version across tiers and pay the cost delta.
[05:00] Sofia Alvarez: We need to quantify cost impact — can you provide a matrix showing p50/p95 latency and cost per 1M tokens across Hosted vs Dedicated vs quantized fallback?
[05:10] Maya Chen: Absolutely — action item. We'll include a scenario tailored to Peregrine's traffic pattern. Liam, do you want to run throughput and cost sims?
[05:17] Liam O'Neill: Yep, I'll run a rough sim based on the numbers Sofia mentioned — I'll include KV cache hit assumptions.
[05:25] Ravi Patel: Also, mention of canary and A/B rollouts — our ops team needs safe canary windows with auto-rollback. How does Redwood handle that?
[05:34] Liam O'Neill: We support canaries and progressive rollouts by percentage or sessions, and if error thresholds are exceeded we auto-roll back. There are hooks for your CI to signal health.
[05:44] Ben Kim: About observability — if a fallback occurs we need token-level tracing retained for 90 days for audits. Does Redwood keep that by default?
[05:53] Maya Chen: By default Hosted retains 30 days; Enterprise add-ons extend retention and provide export hooks to your S3 or logging stores. For Peregrine we can map 90-day retention via an add-on.
[06:05] Sofia Alvarez: Good. On networking: we'll probably keep VPC peering for Dedicated and have egress filters. Any special egress limits or static IPs for outgoing to third parties?
[06:15] Liam O'Neill: We provide static egress IP ranges for enterprise Dedicated and Private. For Hosted there are region egress pools; for strict firewall rules we recommend Dedicated or Private.
[06:25] Ravi Patel: Let's talk incident response — if we see a sev1 on weekdays at 2am, what's primary contact? Is there an on-call rotation?
[06:33] Maya Chen: For enterprise customers with SLA we provide a dedicated escalation path and 24/7 on-call. Otherwise Hosted has business-hours support and pager outside of hours. We'll outline contact model in the contract.
[06:44] Ben Kim: One more technical: if we lose region EU-west, what happens to in-flight KV sessions? Are they replayed or dropped?
[06:52] Liam O'Neill: In-flight sessions are best-effort. We try to drain requests and replicate recent prefix cache to standbys. Some long-running contexts may lose ephemeral state; that's why we recommend idempotent design for critical flows.
[07:08] Ravi Patel: That idempotency requirement is heavy. Any built-in helpers to persist critical state across pools?
[07:15] Liam O'Neill: We offer a session store option persistently stored in your VPC or our encrypted store, which adds a small latency but increases survivability. It's configurable per-route.
[07:26] Sofia Alvarez: Ok helpful. Let's create a candidate pilot: 1 month, dedicated us-east pool (small) + hosted fallthrough, run synthetic traffic simulating market open spikes; define success metrics (p95 <700ms, failover <5s visible error <0.5%).
[07:42] Maya Chen: Sounds good. We'll propose a contract with a 30-day pilot pricing and a checklist of required infra docs.

Documents referenced:
- Pricing & model variants spreadsheet (link): https://redwood.example.com/pilot-pricing/peregrine
- SOC2/ISO excerpt (to be shared): link coming
- Infra diagram request: share via support@redwood.com or drive link

[08:10] Ravi Patel: Okay, last q — if we do private deployment on prem later, how seamless is migration of the routing policies?
[08:19] Liam O'Neill: The control plane configuration is portable; you can export policies and import to private control plane. Data plane differences (latency profiles, kernel opt) will vary, but config-level migration is straightforward.
[08:32] Sofia Alvarez: Great. That addresses most of our worries.

Recap / Next Steps (verbal):
[08:40] Maya Chen: Recap — Redwood to send pilot pricing, routing schematic, SOC2 excerpt. Liam to run throughput sim. Peregrine to send infra diagram and confirm pilot dates. We'll schedule a deeper technical session within next week if possible.

Meeting close: 15:46 UTC

Notes on transcription: speaker attribution approximate; some tech terms may be auto-transcribed incorrectly (e.g., KV cache, canary spelled as 'canary', 'quantization' sometimes 'quanta size').
